claim: Encoding continuous sensory variables requires sustained synaptic signalling.
source: Encoding continuous sensory variables requires sustained synaptic signalling.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory encoding that draws from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: At several sensory synapses, rapid vesicle supply is achieved via highly mobile vesicles and specialized ribbon structures.
source: At several sensory synapses, rapid vesicle supply is achieved via highly mobile vesicles and specialized ribbon structures
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about ribbon synapses in sensory systems.

claim: 75% of VGLUT1-containing vesicles in cerebellar mossy fibre terminals have a high mobility.
source: Fluorescent recovery after photobleaching in slices from VGLUT1Venus knock-in mice reveal 75% of VGLUT1-containing vesicles have a high mobility
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vesicle mobility in cerebellar mossy fibre terminals is comparable to that at ribbon synapses.
source: Fluorescent recovery after photobleaching in slices from VGLUT1Venus knock-in mice reveal 75% of VGLUT1-containing vesicles have a high mobility, comparable to that at ribbon synapses.
evidence: This comparison is supported by the FRAP data and comparison with published values for ribbon synapses.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions are major determinants of vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals.
source: Experimentally constrained models establish hydrodynamic interactions and vesicle collisions are major determinants of vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vesicle collisions are major determinants of vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals.
source: Experimentally constrained models establish hydrodynamic interactions and vesicle collisions are major determinants of vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Models incorporating 3D reconstructions of vesicle clouds near active zones predict the measured releasable pool size.
source: Moreover, models incorporating 3D reconstructions of vesicle clouds near active zones (AZs) predict the measured releasable pool size and replenishment rate from the reserve pool.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results that match experimental measurements.

claim: Models incorporating 3D reconstructions of vesicle clouds near active zones predict the replenishment rate from the reserve pool.
source: Moreover, models incorporating 3D reconstructions of vesicle clouds near active zones (AZs) predict the measured releasable pool size and replenishment rate from the reserve pool.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results that match experimental measurements.

claim: Vesicle reloading at active zones is not diffusion-limited at the onset of release.
source: They also show that while vesicle reloading at AZs is not diffusion-limited at the onset of release, diffusion limits vesicle reloading during sustained high-frequency signalling.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results showing supply rates exceed reloading rates at early times.

claim: Diffusion limits vesicle reloading during sustained high-frequency signalling.
source: They also show that while vesicle reloading at AZs is not diffusion-limited at the onset of release, diffusion limits vesicle reloading during sustained high-frequency signalling.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results showing supply rates match measured release rates at late times.

claim: Information is transmitted at high rates across specialized ribbon synapses at the early stages of auditory, vestibular and visual pathways.
source: At the early stages of auditory, vestibular and visual pathways, information is transmitted at high rates across specialized ribbon synapses (de Ruyter van Steveninck and Laughlin, 1996; Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At ribbon synapses, vesicular release is sustained by a large number of highly mobile vesicles.
source: At these synapses, vesicular release is sustained by a large number of highly mobile vesicles (Holt et al., 2004; Rea et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on ribbon synapses.

claim: A ribbon-like scaffold is thought to rapidly capture and deliver vesicles to the release sites at ribbon synapses.
source: and a ribbon-like scaffold that is thought to rapidly capture and deliver vesicles to the release sites (Griesinger et al., 2005; Khimich et al., 2005; LoGiudice et al., 2008; Graydon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cerebellar mossy fibre terminals have a readily releasable pool (RRP) of only 1–2 vesicles per AZ.
source: Some of these conventional synapses, such as those formed by cerebellar mossy fibre terminals (MFTs) or vestibular nerve fibres, have a readily releasable pool (RRP) of only 1–2 vesicles per AZ, which are docked and primed and ready for release.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about MFT synapses.

claim: A much larger releasable pool (RP) containing 200–300 vesicles resides near the active zone in cerebellar mossy fibre terminals.
source: A much larger releasable pool (RP) containing 200–300 vesicles resides nearby and these vesicles can be supplied to the AZ, docked and primed at a combined rate of 40–80 s−1 (with all three steps referred together as reloading) to refill the RRP (Saviane and Silver, 2006; Hallermann et al., 2010; McElvain et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Vesicles in the releasable pool can be supplied to the AZ, docked and primed at a combined rate of 40–80 s−1 to refill the RRP.
source: A much larger releasable pool (RP) containing 200–300 vesicles resides nearby and these vesicles can be supplied to the AZ, docked and primed at a combined rate of 40–80 s−1 (with all three steps referred together as reloading) to refill the RRP (Saviane and Silver, 2006; Hallermann et al., 2010; McElvain et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Release rates of 7–8 s−1 can be sustained by replenishment from a large vesicle reserve pool at cerebellar mossy fibre terminals during sustained high-frequency stimulation.
source: Even when the large RP is depleted by sustained high-frequency stimulation, release rates of 7–8 s−1 can be sustained by replenishment from a large vesicle reserve pool (R) at these synapses (Saviane and Silver, 2006; McElvain et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Central synapses are thought to contain mostly immobile vesicles.
source: Because these conventional synapses lack ribbons, and central synapses are thought to contain mostly immobile vesicles (Jordan et al., 2005; Lemke and Klingauf, 2005; Shtrahman et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Vesicles are actively transported within axons at ~1–5 µm/s.
source: Vesicles are actively transported within axons at ~1–5 µm/s (Brown, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Passive diffusion is thought to dominate vesicle translocation within the presynaptic terminals of both ribbon and conventional central synapses.
source: but passive diffusion is thought to dominate vesicle translocation within the presynaptic terminals of both ribbon (Holt et al., 2004; Rea et al., 2004; LoGiudice et al., 2008; Graydon et al., 2014) and conventional central synapses (Tokuoka and Goda, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Presynaptic terminals are packed with macromolecules and cytoskeletal elements, as well as vesicles and mitochondria.
source: Presynaptic terminals are packed with macromolecules and cytoskeletal elements, as well as vesicles and mitochondria (Harris and Weinberg, 2012; Wilhelm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The rate of vesicle diffusion is determined by cytoplasmic viscosity, the cytoskeletal matrix, organelles including vesicles, and binding to these elements.
source: The rate of vesicle diffusion will therefore be determined not only by the cytoplasmic viscosity, but by the cytoskeletal matrix (Luby-Phelps et al., 1987) and organelles including vesicles (Gaffield et al., 2006), as well as binding to these elements (Shtrahman et al., 2005) via fine protein connectors (Siksou et al., 2007; Fernández-Busnadiego et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about factors affecting diffusion.

claim: Vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals is substantially lower than that of vesicle-sized beads in cytoplasm.
source: These factors, together with the tortuous paths required to diffuse around large organelles, are thought to explain why vesicle mobility in crowded presynaptic terminals is substantially lower than that of vesicle-sized beads in cytoplasm (Luby-Phelps et al., 1987; Gaffield et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions reduce the mobility of macromolecules in red blood cells and bacteria.
source: Studies of protein diffusion in red blood cells and bacteria (Doster and Longeville, 2007; Ando and Skolnick, 2010) show hydrodynamic interactions reduce the mobility of macromolecules.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions are particularly strong in crowded environments when the volume fraction of the diffusing objects is high.
source: Moreover, studies of colloidal suspensions of vesicle-sized beads demonstrate hydrodynamic interactions are particularly strong in crowded environments, when the volume fraction of the diffusing objects is high (van Blaaderen et al., 1992; Tokuyama and Oppenheim, 1994; Segrè et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on colloidal suspensions.

claim: Nothing is known about how hydrodynamic interactions affect vesicle mobility within axon terminals.
source: However, nothing is known about how hydrodynamic interactions affect vesicle mobility within axon terminals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: EPSC amplitudes, kinetics and short-term plasticity of cerebellar MFT-GC synapses in VGLUT1Venus mice are similar compared to wild-type mice.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from postsynaptic granule cells (GCs) confirmed EPSC amplitudes, kinetics and short-term plasticity of cerebellar MFT-GC synapses in VGLUT1Venus mice were similar compared to wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression and subcellular distribution of VGLUT1Venus is indistinguishable from that of native VGLUT1 in wild-type mice.
source: Moreover, previous work showed the expression and subcellular distribution of VGLUT1Venus is indistinguishable from that of native VGLUT1 in wild-type mice (Herzog et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous publication.

claim: 77% of the bleached fluorescence recovered within 10 s in FRAP experiments on cerebellar mossy fibre terminals.
source: The time of half recovery (t1/2) of the average FRAP curve was 0.8 s and 77% of the bleached fluorescence recovered within 10 s.
evidence: This is directly measured from the FRAP experimental data.

claim: The time of half recovery (t1/2) of the average FRAP curve was 0.8 s.
source: The time of half recovery (t1/2) of the average FRAP curve was 0.8 s and 77% of the bleached fluorescence recovered within 10 s.
evidence: This is directly measured from the FRAP experimental data.

claim: The majority of vesicles within MFTs are highly mobile.
source: These results indicate the majority of vesicles within MFTs are highly mobile.
evidence: This is an inference from the FRAP data showing high fluorescence recovery.

claim: Reducing the temperature from 35° to 21°C slowed the fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments.
source: Reducing the temperature from 35° to 21°C slowed the fluorescence recovery (Figure 2A; f1s = 35 ± 2 vs. 25 ± 3%, respectively, p<0.01; n = 62 vs. 36 MFTs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data at different temperatures.

claim: The Q10 of the t1/2 was 1.5 for vesicle mobility in MFTs.
source: Moreover, the Q10 of the t1/2 was 1.5, which is closer to that expected for passive diffusion (Q10 ~ 1.3) than for active transport in axons (Q10 ~ 3; Forman et al., 1977).
evidence: This is calculated from the temperature-dependent FRAP data and compared to literature values.

claim: Disruption of the actin cytoskeleton with cytochalasin-D and latrunculin-B sped the fluorescence recovery compared to control conditions.
source: Disruption of the actin cytoskeleton with 10 μM cytochalasin-D and 10 μM latrunculin-B (n = 60 MFTs) sped the fluorescence recovery compared to control conditions (f1s = 45 ± 2 vs. 35 ± 2%, respectively, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data with actin-disrupting drugs.

claim: Jasplakinolide slowed fluorescence recovery compared to control conditions.
source: In contrast, 5 μM jasplakinolide (n = 44 MFTs), a peptide that stabilizes actin filaments in vitro (Bubb et al., 2000), slowed fluorescence recovery compared to control conditions (f1s = 27 ± 2 vs. 35 ± 2%, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data with jasplakinolide treatment.

claim: Actin filaments within MFTs have a modest effect on vesicle mobility.
source: These results suggest actin filaments within MFTs (Hirokawa and Yorifuji, 1989) have a modest effect on vesicle mobility.
evidence: This is an inference from the drug manipulation experiments on actin.

claim: Application of okadaic acid dramatically sped the fluorescence recovery.
source: Application of okadaic acid (OA; n = 42 MFTs), a nonspecific phosphatase inhibitor, dramatically sped the fluorescence recovery (Figure 2B; f1s = 64 ± 5 vs. 35 ± 2%, p<0.001, unequal-variance t-test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data with okadaic acid treatment.

claim: Okadaic acid decreased the immobile fraction from 25% to 10–15%.
source: Moreover, OA decreased the immobile fraction from 25% to 10–15%, indicating the immobile fraction can be attributed to immobile vesicles rather than large immobile organelles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data with okadaic acid treatment.

claim: Roscovitine had no detectable effect on the rate of fluorescence recovery.
source: We found 50 µM roscovitine had no detectable effect on the rate of fluorescence recovery (Figure 2B; f1s = 38 ± 3 vs. 35 ± 2%, p=0.3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data with roscovitine treatment.

claim: There is little synapsin-based vesicle clustering at the centre of MFTs.
source: suggesting that, as for ribbon synapses (Mandell et al., 1990), there is little synapsin-based vesicle clustering at the centre of MFTs.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of effect of roscovitine, compared to ribbon synapses.

claim: Fluorescence recovery was nearly absent in paraformaldehyde-fixed slices.
source: Finally, we repeated our FRAP experiments using paraformaldehyde-fixed slices (n = 17 MFTs), where subcellular components, including vesicles, were immobilized by cross-linking, and found fluorescence recovery was nearly absent (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRAP data on fixed tissue.

claim: FRAP measurements reflect the diffusion of vesicles within MFTs.
source: Together, these results confirm our FRAP measurements reflect the diffusion of vesicles within MFTs
evidence: This is an inference from the various control experiments and manipulations.

claim: Vesicle mobility is reduced by the presence of a network of actin filaments in the cytoplasm.
source: suggest vesicle mobility is reduced by the presence of a network of actin filaments in the cytoplasm
evidence: This is an inference from the actin manipulation experiments.

claim: Synapsin has little impact on vesicle mobility within the interior of MFTs.
source: and indicate synapsin has little impact on vesicle mobility within the interior of MFTs.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of effect of roscovitine.

claim: The long-time self-diffusion coefficient (Dlong) of vesicles in MFTs is 0.018 ± 0.005 µm2/s for the raw control FRAP curve.
source: This gave Dlong = 0.018 ± 0.005 µm2/s for the raw control FRAP curve
evidence: This is calculated by fitting the FRAP data to an analytical diffusion model.

claim: The long-time self-diffusion coefficient (Dlong) of vesicles in MFTs is 0.025 ± 0.003 µm2/s after correcting for tissue drift.
source: and 0.025 ± 0.003 µm2/s after correcting for tissue drift (Figure 2C, red line; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated by fitting the drift-corrected FRAP data to an analytical diffusion model.

claim: Diffusion underlies vesicle mobility in MFTs.
source: Moreover, the fit of the weighted sum of the diffusion and flow models converged on diffusion (98%), suggesting diffusion underlies vesicle mobility in MFTs.
evidence: This is an inference from model fitting to the FRAP data.

claim: Vesicle mobility is higher in MFTs than at other conventional central synapses and the neuromuscular junction.
source: A comparison of our best estimate for Dlong in MFTs (0.025 µm2/s) with that estimated at other synapses (Figure 2D) indicates vesicle mobility is higher in MFTs than at other conventional central synapses and the neuromuscular junction (NMJ)
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured Dlong value with published values for other synapses.

claim: Vesicle density is 3930 ± 262 per µm3 in regions not occupied by mitochondria in the central region of MFTs.
source: Quantitative analysis of 3D volumes (0.2–0.4 µm3, n = 3) revealed a vesicle density of 3930 ± 262 per µm3 (or 118 ± 8 per µm2 in 2D) in regions not occupied by mitochondria
evidence: This is measured from serial-section EM data.

claim: The mean vesicle diameter is 41.1 ± 0.2 nm in MFTs.
source: Vesicle diameters exhibited an approximately normal distribution with a mean of 41.1 ± 0.2 nm (256 vesicles around 3 AZs; Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is measured from high-resolution 3D electron tomography.

claim: The mean volume occupied by a vesicle is equivalent to a sphere with 44 nm diameter.
source: Taking into account vesicle membrane proteins (Takamori et al., 2006), and the cubic relationship between vesicle radius and volume, indicates the mean volume occupied by a vesicle is equivalent to a sphere with 44 nm diameter.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured vesicle diameter and accounting for membrane proteins.

claim: The vesicle volume fraction is 0.17 ± 0.01 of the non-mitochondrial volume in the central region of MFTs.
source: Using this diameter, we computed a vesicle volume fraction of 0.17 ± 0.01 of the non-mitochondrial volume (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is calculated from the vesicle density and diameter measurements.

claim: The average volume fraction occupied by mitochondria is 0.28 ± 0.04 in the central region of MFTs.
source: The average volume fraction occupied by mitochondria was 0.28 ± 0.04.
evidence: This is measured from serial-section EM data.

claim: 40% of the volume in the central region of the MFT is occupied by vesicles and mitochondria.
source: Hence, this analysis shows the central region of the MFT is a highly crowded environment with 40% of the volume occupied by vesicles and mitochondria.
evidence: This is calculated from the vesicle and mitochondria volume fraction measurements.

claim: The best-match Monte Carlo simulation has Dshort = 0.060 µm2/s and a 25% immobile vesicle fraction.
source: The log of the χ2 calculated from the simulated and experimental FRAP curves had a minimum at Dshort = 0.060 µm2/s and a 25% immobile fraction (68.3% confidence intervals 0.055–0.070 µm2/s and 24–25%, respectively).
evidence: This is determined by parameter search to match experimental FRAP data.

claim: Over the 10 s period of the FRAP experiment, D(t) reached a steady-state value of 0.025 µm2/s.
source: At longer times, however, as vesicles collided with themselves and mitochondria, D(t) fell to a steady-state value of 0.025 µm2/s.
evidence: This is calculated from the Monte Carlo simulation results.

claim: Over long timescales vesicle collisions reduce vesicle mobility by a factor of 2.4.
source: These results indicate steric interactions introduce a pronounced time dependence to vesicle diffusion and over long timescales vesicle collisions reduce vesicle mobility by a factor of 2.4 (i.e. Dlong/Dshort = 0.42).
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of Dlong to Dshort from the simulation results.

claim: For conditions within MFTs, the reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions between mobile vesicles was 30%.
source: For conditions within MFTs, the reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions between mobile vesicles was 30%, while that due to collisions with immobile vesicles and mitochondria was 13% and 32%, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the Monte Carlo simulation results exploring different conditions.

claim: The reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions with immobile vesicles was 13% for conditions within MFTs.
source: For conditions within MFTs, the reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions between mobile vesicles was 30%, while that due to collisions with immobile vesicles and mitochondria was 13% and 32%, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the Monte Carlo simulation results exploring different conditions.

claim: The reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions with mitochondria was 32% for conditions within MFTs.
source: For conditions within MFTs, the reduction in vesicle mobility due to collisions between mobile vesicles was 30%, while that due to collisions with immobile vesicles and mitochondria was 13% and 32%, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the Monte Carlo simulation results exploring different conditions.

claim: Vesicle collisions are a major determinant of vesicle mobility at a central synaptic terminal.
source: These results show vesicle collisions are a major determinant of vesicle mobility at a central synaptic terminal.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing the magnitude of the effect.

claim: For the vesicle volume fraction found at the centre of MFTs, Dshort/Dcyto = 0.47.
source: For the vesicle volume fraction found at the centre of MFTs, Dshort/Dcyto = 0.47 (dashed blue line) suggesting hydrodynamic interactions reduce vesicle mobility by two-fold within MFTs.
evidence: This is calculated using analytical expressions for hydrodynamic interactions.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions reduce vesicle mobility by two-fold within MFTs.
source: For the vesicle volume fraction found at the centre of MFTs, Dshort/Dcyto = 0.47 (dashed blue line) suggesting hydrodynamic interactions reduce vesicle mobility by two-fold within MFTs.
evidence: This is an inference from the calculated Dshort/Dcyto ratio.

claim: For the conditions at the centre of MFTs, the combined effect of hydrodynamic interactions and vesicle collisions resulted in an 80% reduction in vesicle mobility (Dlong/Dcyto = 0.19).
source: For the conditions at the centre of MFTs, the combined effect of hydrodynamic interactions and vesicle collisions resulted in an 80% reduction in vesicle mobility (Dlong/Dcyto = 0.19; dashed blue line).
evidence: This is calculated by combining the effects of hydrodynamic and steric interactions.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of dilute vesicles in cytoplasm, in the absence of crowding effects, is 0.127 µm2/s.
source: This suggests the diffusion coefficient of dilute vesicles in cytoplasm, in the absence of crowding effects, is 0.127 µm2/s
evidence: This is calculated by accounting for the crowding effects on the measured Dlong.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of dilute vesicles in cytoplasm is only a factor of 3.5 lower than that of dilute 50 nm beads in the cytoplasm of 3T3 cells at 37°C.
source: which is only a factor of 3.5 lower than that of dilute 50 nm beads in the cytoplasm of 3T3 cells at 37°C (0.45 µm2/s; Luby-Phelps et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a comparison with published values for bead diffusion.

claim: A likely explanation of the lower value of Dcyto for vesicles than beads is that vesicle protein interactions with the cytomatrix slow vesicle mobility.
source: A likely explanation of the lower value of Dcyto for vesicles than beads is that vesicle protein interactions with the cytomatrix slow vesicle mobility.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: The AZ area varied across synaptic contacts from 0.009–0.039 µm2 with a mean of 0.017 ± 0.002 µm2 (n = 14).
source: The AZ area, closely opposed to the postsynaptic density, varied across synaptic contacts (0.009–0.039 µm2) with a mean of 0.017 ± 0.002 µm2 (n = 14).
evidence: This is measured from 3D reconstructions of serial-section EM data.

claim: The AZ area at MFTs is smaller than most other central synapses which can have 10-fold larger areas.
source: This is smaller than most other central synapses which can have 10-fold larger areas (Xu-Friedman and Regehr, 2004; Harris and Weinberg, 2012; Holderith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with published values for other synapses.

claim: The mean AZ diameter corresponds to 145 ± 8 nm when expressed as the diameter of a circular disk.
source: When expressed as the diameter of a circular disk, our AZ measurements correspond to a range of 108–222 nm, with mean 145 ± 8 nm.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured AZ area.

claim: Vesicle density reached 5652 ± 377 per µm3 at 30 nm from the AZ.
source: The vesicle density reached 5652 ± 377 per µm3 at 30 nm from the AZ.
evidence: This is measured from 3D reconstructions of vesicle positions near AZs.

claim: Vesicle density at 30 nm from the AZ corresponds to a volume fraction of 0.25.
source: This corresponds to a volume fraction of 0.25, assuming a vesicle diameter of 44 nm in fixed tissue, which is 50% higher than the volume fraction at the center of MFTs (0.17).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured vesicle density.

claim: Vesicle density declined with distance from the AZ, converging to the density estimated at the centre of the MFT for distances >100 nm.
source: Vesicle density declined with distance from the AZ, converging to the density estimated at the centre of the MFT for distances >100 nm.
evidence: This is measured from 3D reconstructions of vesicle positions near AZs.

claim: An accumulation of vesicles extends ~2 vesicle diameters from the AZ.
source: These results suggest an accumulation of vesicles extends ~2 vesicle diameters from the AZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the vesicle density measurements as a function of distance from the AZ.

claim: The total number of vesicles increased monotonically with distance from the AZ, from 2 ± 1 within 22 nm, to 48 ± 6 within 100 nm and 252 ± 34 within 300 nm.
source: The total number of vesicles increased monotonically with distance from the AZ, from 2 ± 1 within 22 nm, to 48 ± 6 within 100 nm and 252 ± 34 within 300 nm (Figure 6C, top).
evidence: This is measured from 3D reconstructions of vesicle positions near AZs.

claim: While there are few docked vesicles at the AZ, hundreds of vesicles reside nearby.
source: These results show that, while there are few docked vesicles at the AZ, hundreds of vesicles reside nearby.
evidence: This is an inference from the vesicle count measurements as a function of distance from the AZ.

claim: Diffusional barriers imposed by intracellular organelles and/or the plasma membrane are present in the AZ region.
source: The similarity in vesicle density within the cloud and in the MFT interior (Figure 6C, bottom; red circles and dashed horizontal line, respectively), plus the irregular shape of the vesicle clouds, suggests diffusional barriers imposed by intracellular organelles and/or the plasma membrane are present in the AZ region.
evidence: This is an inference from the vesicle density measurements and cloud shapes.

claim: Mitochondria are located within 270 ± 20 nm (n = 29) of the AZ.
source: Indeed, quantification of the mean distance from the AZ to the nearest mitochondrial membrane revealed mitochondria are located within 270 ± 20 nm (n = 29) of the AZ.
evidence: This is measured from the 3D reconstructions.

claim: The diffusible space available to vesicles is restricted near the AZ of MFTs.
source: These results suggest that the diffusible space available to vesicles is restricted near the AZ of MFTs
evidence: This is an inference from the vesicle density measurements and proximity of mitochondria.

claim: At the earliest simulation times (0–2 ms) the vesicle supply rate varied between 25–4000 s−1, with a mean of ~1000 s−1.
source: At the earliest simulation times (0–2 ms) the vesicle supply rate varied between 25–4000 s−1, with a mean of ~1000 s−1 (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulations of vesicle diffusion at reconstructed AZs.

claim: The average vesicle supply rate declined to ~200 s−1 by 10 ms when ~5 vesicles had been released.
source: The average vesicle supply rate declined to ~200 s−1 by 10 ms when ~5 vesicles had been released (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulations of vesicle diffusion at reconstructed AZs.

claim: Vesicle supply rates at early times are well above the experimental vesicle reloading rates of 40–80 s−1 per functional release site.
source: These values are well above the experimental vesicle reloading rates of 40–80 s−1 per functional release site estimated at MFT-GC synapses during brief bursts of high-frequency stimulation (Saviane and Silver, 2006; Hallermann et al., 2010) and obtained during continuous depolarization of the presynaptic terminal (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results with published experimental measurements.

claim: At early times vesicle diffusion does not limit vesicle reloading at the AZ.
source: These results suggest that at early times vesicle diffusion does not limit vesicle reloading at the AZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of simulated supply rates with experimental reloading rates.

claim: The slope of the linear portion of the cumulative supply functions gave a mean vesicle supply rate of 7 ± 1 s−1 at late times (50–100 s).
source: The slope of the linear portion of the cumulative supply functions gave a mean vesicle supply rate of 7 ± 1 s−1 (Figure 7G,H)
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulations of vesicle diffusion at reconstructed AZs.

claim: The mean vesicle supply rate of 7 ± 1 s−1 at late times is remarkably similar to the vesicle release rates per release site measured at MFTs (8 s−1) and vestibular nerve synapses (7 s−1) during long trains of stimuli.
source: which is remarkably similar to the vesicle release rates per release site measured at MFTs (8 s−1; Saviane and Silver, 2006) and vestibular nerve synapses (7 s−1; McElvain et al., 2015) during long trains of stimuli.
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results with published experimental measurements.

claim: The back-extrapolation method for estimating the size of the pool of vesicles that can be depleted during the train gave an average of 237 ± 40 vesicles.
source: Moreover, the back-extrapolation method for estimating the size of the pool of vesicles that can be depleted during the train (i.e. RRP+RP) gave an average of 237 ± 40 vesicles (Figure 7I)
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulations of vesicle diffusion at reconstructed AZs.

claim: The pool size estimate of 237 ± 40 vesicles is similar to values obtained for EPSC trains at MFTs (300) and vestibular nerve synapses (200).
source: similar to values obtained for EPSC trains at MFTs (300; Saviane and Silver, 2006) and vestibular nerve synapses (200; McElvain et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results with published experimental measurements.

claim: Vesicular release is diffusion-limited during sustained high-frequency signalling once the RRP and RP are depleted.
source: The close agreement between our experimentally constrained models of vesicle diffusion at AZs and experimental measurements suggests vesicular release is diffusion-limited during sustained high-frequency signalling once the RRP and RP are depleted.
evidence: This is an inference from the agreement between simulation and experimental results.

claim: Vesicle density close to the AZ falls dramatically during sustained release, reaching a steady state after ~20 s.
source: Examination of vesicle density close to the AZ during sustained release revealed that it falls dramatically, reaching a steady state after ~20 s (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, control conditions).
evidence: This is observed in the Monte Carlo simulations.

claim: Vesicle mobility increased substantially during vesicle depletion due to reduced hydrodynamic and steric interactions.
source: However, vesicle mobility increased substantially during vesicle depletion due to reduced hydrodynamic and steric interactions, resulting in a shallow concentration gradient and a constant vesicle supply rate at late times.
evidence: This is observed in the Monte Carlo simulations.

claim: Fast hydrodynamic interactions between vesicles play a key role in slowing vesicle supply to the AZ.
source: This increased the vesicle supply rate at early, intermediate and late times (Figure 7C–E,H), indicating fast hydrodynamic interactions between vesicles play a key role in slowing vesicle supply to the AZ.
evidence: This is an inference from simulations with and without hydrodynamic interactions.

claim: At late times, removing vesicle collisions increased vesicle supply to the AZ by a factor of 2.
source: However, at late times, removing vesicle collisions increased vesicle supply to the AZ by a factor of 2 (Figure 7C,G,H)
evidence: This is calculated from simulations with and without steric interactions.

claim: The physical interactions arising from vesicle crowding limit the maximal vesicle supply rate to the AZ.
source: These results show the physical interactions arising from vesicle crowding limit the maximal vesicle supply rate to the AZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing the effects of removing these interactions.

claim: For open geometries, the average vesicle supply rate at early times was the same as that for the control geometries.
source: For open geometries, the average vesicle supply rate at early times was the same as that for the control geometries (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is calculated from simulations with open geometries.

claim: The presence of diffusion boundaries arising from membrane invaginations, intracellular organelles and possibly the actin cytomatrix limit diffusion-mediated vesicle supply to the AZ.
source: These results suggest the presence of diffusion boundaries arising from membrane invaginations, intracellular organelles and possibly the actin cytomatrix (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003; Guillet et al., 2016) limit diffusion-mediated vesicle supply to the AZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of control and open geometry simulations.

claim: The geometry of the diffusible space close to the AZ determines the size of the functionally defined RP.
source: Moreover, by determining the limiting vesicle supply rate during sustained release and thus the size of the pool of vesicles that can be depleted before release and supply rates equalize (excluding those replenished during that time), the geometry of the diffusible space close to the AZ determines the size of the functionally defined RP.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing the effect of geometry on pool size.

claim: At later times during the train (>1 s), the release rate converged with that for instantaneous release, indicating that it had become limited by the diffusion-mediated vesicle supply.
source: However, at later times during the train (>1 s), the release rate converged with that for instantaneous release, indicating that it had become limited by the diffusion-mediated vesicle supply (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is observed in simulations of 100 Hz trains with docking/priming delays.

claim: Back extrapolation analysis of cumulative release at late times during the 100 Hz train gave estimates for the limiting vesicle release rate and RP size that were similar to that obtained with instantaneous release.
source: Back extrapolation analysis of cumulative release at late times during the 100 Hz train gave estimates for the limiting vesicle release rate and RP size that were similar to that obtained with instantaneous release, irrespective of whether 1 or 2 release sites were present (Figure 8D,F,G).
evidence: This is calculated from simulations of 100 Hz trains with docking/priming delays.

claim: Vesicle release becomes diffusion-limited during sustained high-frequency signalling.
source: These more realistic simulations of release during 100 Hz trains therefore support our finding that vesicle release becomes diffusion-limited during sustained high-frequency signalling.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulations of 100 Hz trains with docking/priming delays.

source: show vesicle mobility at an excitatory central synapse is comparable to that at ribbon synapses

claim: Results provide a structural basis for the functionally defined ~300 vesicle RP at MFT AZs.
source: Moreover, our results provide a structural basis for the functionally defined ~300 vesicle RP at MFT AZs.

claim: Crowding within presynaptic terminals gives rise to two types of physical interaction that slow vesicle mobility: fast hydrodynamic interactions and vesicle collisions.
source: Our results show that crowding within presynaptic terminals gives rise to two types of physical interaction that slow vesicle mobility. Fast hydrodynamic interactions arising from fluid displacement influence vesicle mobility on both short (microsecond) and long (millisecond to second) timescales. In contrast, effects of vesicle collisions (Gaffield et al., 2006) are only felt on long time scales.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results on physical interactions.

claim: The combined effects of hydrodynamic and steric interactions result in a vesicle diffusion coefficient that evolves with a characteristic time course that depends on the vesicle density.
source: The combined effects of these interactions result in a vesicle diffusion coefficient that evolves with a characteristic time course that depends on the vesicle density (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions are likely to be a major determinant of vesicle diffusion in synaptic terminals.
source: Our results extend these studies by showing hydrodynamic interactions are likely to be a major determinant of vesicle diffusion in synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results showing the magnitude of the effect.

claim: Taking account of hydrodynamic and steric interactions arising from vesicle crowding explains much of the discrepancy between Dlong of vesicles and 50 nm beads in cytoplasm.
source: Indeed, taking account of hydrodynamic and steric interactions arising from vesicle crowding explains much of the discrepancy between Dlong of vesicles and 50 nm beads in cytoplasm (Luby-Phelps et al., 1987).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results and comparison with published data.

claim: The quantitative model of vesicle mobility predicts that vesicle diffusion slows down from 0.025 μm2/s within the MFT interior to 0.012 μm2/s in the vicinity of the AZ.
source: At MFTs our quantitative model of vesicle mobility predicts that vesicle diffusion slows down from 0.025 μm2/s within the MFT interior to 0.012 μm2/s in the vicinity of the AZ.
evidence: This is calculated from the model of vesicle mobility applied to the measured vesicle densities.

claim: Physical interactions slow vesicle mobility even in the absence of binding to tethers and connectors.
source: Thus, physical interactions slow vesicle mobility even in the absence of binding to tethers and connectors (which could slow diffusion further to 0.002 μm2/s).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: For ribbon-type bipolar cells, the model of vesicle mobility predicts Dlong = 0.014 μm2/s, which matches well to the value measured in goldfish (0.015 μm2/s).
source: For ribbon-type bipolar cells, which have a vesicle density comparable to MFTs, our model of vesicle mobility predicts Dlong = 0.014 μm2/s, which matches well to the value measured in goldfish (0.015 μm2/s; Holt et al., 2004)
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with published experimental data.

claim: The framework predicts the low vesicle mobility at the NMJ (predicted 0.006 μm2/s vs. measured 0.005 μm2/s).
source: Nevertheless, our framework does predict the low vesicle mobility at the NMJ (predicted 0.006 μm2/s vs. measured 0.005 μm2/s; Gaffield and Betz, 2007)
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with published experimental data.

claim: Modelling predicts that Dlong is low within the middle of the vesicle cluster in small boutons (0.002 μm2/s).
source: Our modelling predicts that Dlong is low within the middle of the vesicle cluster in small boutons (0.002 μm2/s).
evidence: This is calculated from the model of vesicle mobility applied to estimated vesicle densities in small boutons.

claim: Synapsin-based immobilization of vesicles appears prevalent in small boutons.
source: Synapsin-based immobilization of vesicles appears prevalent in small boutons (Orenbuch et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There is a rapid vesicle exchange with the axon where mobility is high in small boutons.
source: Moreover, there is a rapid vesicle exchange with the axon (Staras et al., 2010; Herzog et al., 2011) where mobility is high (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The low mobility of vesicles in small central synapses is largely due to strong steric and hydrodynamic interactions arising from the high vesicle density.
source: Our simulations suggest that the low mobility of vesicles in small central synapses is largely due to strong steric and hydrodynamic interactions arising from the high vesicle density.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Although the presence of tethers/connectors will restrict vesicle mobility further, their effects will only be strong if they have long lifetimes.
source: Moreover, although the presence of tethers/connectors will restrict vesicle mobility further, their effects will only be strong if they have long lifetimes (i.e. slow unbinding).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results with connectors/tethers.

claim: To understand the variations in vesicle mobility across synapses, it is necessary to account for the physical interactions arising from organelle crowding.
source: While the properties of vesicle mobility within small synapses is still uncertain, our results show that to understand the variations in vesicle mobility across synapses, it is necessary to account for the physical interactions arising from organelle crowding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings.
